```
138: In the contemporary cybersecurity landscape, Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are consistently overwhelmed by the sheer volume of network alerts, leading to severe alert fatigue and the potential oversight of critical Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs). To address the inherent limitations of traditional, static rule-based systems and the latency bottlenecks of processing raw logs directly through Large Language Models (LLMs), this thesis introduces SENTINEL: A Two-Tier Cognitive Architecture for Automated Threat Detection and Response. The proposed framework operates by deploying Welford's online statistical algorithm at the Transport Tier (Tier-1) to filter benign traffic at wire speed with minimal computational overhead. Subsequently, the Cognitive Agent Tier (Tier-2) leverages a LangGraph-driven AI Agent equipped with a Dual Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Dual-RAG) mechanism—integrating MITRE ATT\&CK and NIST guidelines—to perform deep, contextual threat reasoning and mitigation. 
139: 
140: Evaluated on the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 and DAPT2020 datasets, SENTINEL demonstrates substantial improvements in both detection accuracy and processing efficiency. Furthermore, the system incorporates robust AI security guardrails, including Delimited Data Encapsulation and HMAC log chaining, achieving near-perfect mitigation against known adversarial AI manipulation attacks and ensuring forensic data integrity. The findings underscore the efficacy of combining deterministic statistical filters with explainable Agentic AI, offering a highly scalable and secure automation solution for modern network defense.
```

```
6: \title{\bfseries Endogenous Investment and Capital Accumulation\\[2pt]
7:        in a Disaggregated Keynesian Cross\\[6pt]
8:        \large A Normalised-CES Agent-Based Model with an Endogenous
9:        Labour Market}
10: 
11: \author{%
12:   Mattia \textsc{[Surname]}\thanks{%
13:   Correspondence: \texttt{[email]}. This paper documents an exploratory
14:   computational model. Every number reported here is either \emph{measured}
15:   from a committed, reproducible driver script, or explicitly declared as a
16:   design target or convention; the distinction is maintained throughout
17:   (\cref{sec:method}). Code, data and figures:
18:   \texttt{[repository URL]}.}\\[2pt]
19:   \normalsize [Institution]}
20: 
21: \date{\today}
22: 
23: \maketitle
24: 
25: 
26: \begin{abstract}
27: \noindent
28: We extend the disaggregated Keynesian cross of \citet{Teglio2025} with
29: endogenous investment and capital accumulation, so that both the demand and
30: the supply side of a heterogeneous-agent economy are endogenous. Production
31: is a \emph{normalised} CES \citep{KlumpDeLaGrandville2000} with elasticity of
32: substitution~$\sigma$; firms hire endogenously subject to three limits, the
33: wage follows a Blanchflower--Oswald wage curve, investment is financed
34: internally out of retained earnings, and the model is stock-flow consistent
35: across the whole parameter space. The central question is Kaleckian: does
36: higher retention raise output by building capacity (supply), or lower it by
37: displacing workers and shrinking the wage bill (demand)?
38: 
39: We find that the answer is governed by~$\sigma$, but that it is not well posed
40: as a single label. $Y(\rho)$ is \emph{U-shaped}, with a turning point
41: $\rhostar$ that rises with~$\sigma$ and lies inside the swept support in 19 of
42: 22 conditional cells; the empirically anchored retention rate lies to the
43: \emph{left} of that turn for every $\sigma \geq 0.5$, so retention depresses
44: output there and expands it beyond. Read through a single slope, this
45: structure presents as a \emph{sign frontier} $\sigstar \approx 0.65$ --- a
46: description we retain, but as a local summary of a curve rather than as a
47: verdict on the economy. Three separate stabilisation hypotheses --- slower demand
48: expectations, a balanced-budget unemployment benefit, and that same benefit
49: as a cushion against firm heterogeneity --- are each \emph{falsified} by the
50: data they were designed to test, and all three fail through the same channel:
51: a wage$\,\to\,$unemployment$\,\to\,$capital-erosion feedback that originates
52: in the wage curve and is immune to demand-side instruments. This channel,
53: rather than the sign frontier, is the model's most robust finding.
54: 
55: A global sensitivity analysis over sixteen parameters then shows that the
56: headline does \emph{not} survive marginalisation: wage-led outcomes are the
57: exception, only $48\%$ of the empirically defensible space is viable at all,
58: and viability is governed almost entirely by the depreciation rate $\delta$
59: ($S_T \approx 1.00$) rather than by~$\sigma$ ($S_T = 0.02$). At the
60: depreciation rate the data imply for this model's perimeter
61: ($\delta \approx 0.09$), \emph{zero} of 843 sampled points survive --- a
62: structural limitation of a capital block without trend growth, not a parameter
63: to be tuned.
64: 
65: Finally we show that the quantity of interest was itself part of the result. A
66: $2\times2$ experiment, under a verdict rule fixed in advance, separates the two
67: candidate explanations of the gap between the conditional and marginal
68: readings, and returns the estimator: measuring a two-point chord across a
69: U-shaped response rather than a slope over its whole support moves $\sigstar$
70: from $0.643$ to $0.447$ on identical data, with non-overlapping intervals.
71: Re-running the entire sensitivity analysis on the repaired quantity cuts
72: $P(\text{wage-led} \mid \text{viable})$ from $0.095$ to $0.026$, while leaving
73: the variance decomposition almost unchanged --- \emph{which} parameters matter
74: is robust to the estimator, the \emph{level} of the headline is not. We also
75: document, and correct, a reading error of our own: an apparent inversion of
76: sign between the conditional and marginal analyses, which we had reported as
77: an open contradiction, was never present in the measurements.
78: 
79: \bigskip
80: \noindent\textbf{Keywords:} agent-based macroeconomics; stock-flow
81: consistency; elasticity of substitution; wage-led growth; global sensitivity
82: analysis; capital accumulation.
```

```
2: %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
3: % Introduction
4: %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
5: 
6: \section{Introduction}
7: \label{sec:intro}
8: 
9: The disaggregated Keynesian cross of \citet{Teglio2025} shows how
10: heterogeneity in the marginal propensity to consume opens an output gap: when
11: income accrues to agents who do not spend it, demand leaks out of the
12: circular flow and the economy settles below capacity. The mechanism is a
13: demand mechanism, and the supply side plays no active role: capacity is given.
14: 
15: This paper asks what happens when the supply side is made endogenous in the
16: most direct way available --- by letting firms invest out of their own
17: profits and accumulate capital. The extension is not merely additive. Once
18: capital accumulates \emph{and} labour is hired endogenously, two channels
19: that point in opposite directions become active simultaneously:
20: 
21: \begin{itemize}
22:   \item \textbf{Supply.} Higher retention $\rho$ means more investment, more
23:   capital, and higher productive capacity. Taken alone, this raises output.
24:   \item \textbf{Demand.} In a demand-constrained regime, more capital means
25:   \emph{fewer workers are needed to serve the same demand}. Employment falls,
26:   the wage bill falls, and because workers have a higher propensity to consume
27:   than capitalists, demand falls with it.
28: \end{itemize}
29: 
30: Which channel dominates is the classical wage-led versus profit-led question
31: \citep{BhaduriMarglin1990,LavoieStockhammer2013}, and this paper's first
32: result is that its answer is not a property of the model but a function of a
33: single technological parameter: the elasticity of substitution between
34: capital and labour, $\sigma$.
35: 
36: \paragraph{Three contributions.}
37: First, we build and calibrate a stock-flow-consistent agent-based model in
38: which the wage-led/profit-led sign is an \emph{outcome} rather than an
39: assumption, and we locate the frontier $\sigstar$ at which it turns
40: (\cref{sec:frontier}). Second, we subject that frontier to four independent
41: stress tests --- wage flexibility, adaptive expectations, fiscal policy, and
42: firm heterogeneity --- and report that three explicit stabilisation
43: hypotheses are falsified, all three through the same
44: wage$\,\to\,U\,\to\,$capital-erosion channel (\cref{sec:stress},
45: \cref{sec:discussion}). Third, we run a global sensitivity analysis over the
46: full defensible parameter space and find that the headline result does not
47: survive marginalisation, that viability is governed by the depreciation rate
48: rather than by $\sigma$, and that at the empirically implied depreciation
49: rate the model does not exist at all (\cref{sec:sa}).
50: 
51: \paragraph{A note on what this paper reports.}
52: An unusual proportion of what follows is negative. Three hypotheses are
53: falsified; one headline is shown not to generalise; one contradiction is left
54: explicitly open. This is deliberate. The project operates under a declared
55: rule --- restated in \cref{sec:method} --- that every number entering a table
56: or a figure must either be measured from a committed, reproducible driver or
57: be labelled a design target. The rule was adopted after an audit found that
58: several previously recorded ``results'' were in fact design targets that had
59: never been measured. Its consequence is that results which contradict the
60: project's own expectations are reported rather than recalibrated away, and
61: the reader should read the negative findings as the paper's substance, not
62: as its residue.
63: 
64: The remainder is organised as follows. \Cref{sec:literature} places the model
65: in the literature. \Cref{sec:model} presents it. \Cref{sec:calibration}
66: documents parameter anchoring, distinguishing estimates from conventions.
67: \Cref{sec:method} states the experimental protocol. \Cref{sec:baseline} to
68: \cref{sec:sa} report results. \Cref{sec:discussion} draws the two
69: cross-cutting readings, \cref{sec:limits} states the limitations, and
70: \cref{sec:conclusion} concludes.
71: 
```

```
207:         To meet the need for a cross-platform, versatile and easy-to-use listening test tool, we previously developed the Web Audio Evaluation Tool \cite{waet} which at the time of its inception was capable of running a listening test in the browser from an XML configuration file, and storing an XML file as well, with one particular interface. Specifically, in Section \ref{sec:architecture} we cover the general implementation aspects, with a focus on the Web Audio API, followed by a discussion of the requirements for successful remote tests in Section \ref{sec:remote}. Section \ref{sec:interfaces} describes the various interfaces the tool supports, as well as how to keep this manageable. Finally, in Section \ref{sec:analysis} we provide an overview of the analysis capabilities in the browser, before summarising our findings and listing future research directions in Section \ref{sec:conclusion}.
```

```
132: \section{Introduction}
133: 
134: 	% Listening tests/perceptual audio evaluation: what are they, why are they important
135: 	% As opposed to limited scope of WAC15 paper: also musical features, realism of sound effects / sound synthesis, performance of source separation and other algorithms... 
136: 	Perceptual evaluation of audio, in the form of listening tests, is a powerful way to assess anything from audio codec quality over realism of sound synthesis to the performance of source separation, automated music production and other auditory evaluations.
137: 	In less technical areas, the framework of a listening test can be used to measure emotional response to music or test cognitive abilities. 
138: 	% maybe some references? If there's space.
139: 
140: 	% check out http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10055-015-0270-8 - only paper that cited WAC15 paper
141: 
142: 	% Why difficult? Challenges? What constitutes a good interface?
143: 	% Technical, interfaces, user friendliness, reliability 
144: 	Several applications for performing perceptual listening tests currently exist, as can be seen in Table \ref{tab:toolboxes}. The Web Audio Evaluation Toolbox stands out as it does not require proprietary software or a specific platform and provides a wide range of interface and test types in one user friendly environment. Furthermore, it does not require any progamming experience as any test based on the default test types can be configured in the browser as well. Note that the design of an effective listening test further poses many challenges unrelated to interface design, which are beyond the scope of this paper \cite{bech}. 
145: 
146: 	% Why in the browser? 
147: 	Web Audio API has important features for performing perceptual tests including sample level manipulation of audio streams \cite{schoeffler2015mushra}, synchronous playback and flexible playback. Being in the browser also allows leveraging the flexible object oriented JavaScript format and native support for web documents, such as the extensible markup language (XML) which is used for configuration and test result files. Using the web also reduces deployment requirements to a basic web server with advanced functionality such as test collection and automatic processing using PHP. As recruiting participants can be very time-consuming, and as for some tests a large number of participants is needed, browser-based tests \cite{schoeffler2015mushra}. However, to our knowledge, no tool currently exists that allows the creation of a remotely accessible listening test. 
148:

205:         %Selling points: remote tests, visualisaton, create your own test in the browser, many interfaces, few/no dependencies, flexibility
206: 
207:         To meet the need for a cross-platform, versatile and easy-to-use listening test tool, we previously developed the Web Audio Evaluation Tool \cite{waet} which at the time of its inception was capable of running a listening test in the browser from an XML configuration file, and storing an XML file as well, with one particular interface. We have now expanded this into a tool with which a wide range of listening test types can easily be constructed and set up remotely, without any need for manually altering code or configuration files, and which allows visualisation of the collected results in the browser. In this paper, we discuss these different aspects and explore which future improvements would be possible. Specifically, in Section \ref{sec:architecture} we cover the general implementation aspects, with a focus on the Web Audio API, followed by a discussion of the requirements for successful remote tests in Section \ref{sec:remote}. Section \ref{sec:interfaces} describes the various interfaces the tool supports, as well as how to keep this manageable. Finally, in Section \ref{sec:analysis} we provide an overview of the analysis capabilities in the browser, before summarising our findings and listing future research directions in Section \ref{sec:conclusion}.

239: 
240:     While WAET uses a sparse subset of the Web Audio API functionality, its performance comes directly from using the Web Audio API for audio playback. Listening tests can convey large amounts of information other than obtaining the perceptual relationship between the audio fragments. Specifically, with WAET one can obtain which parts of the audio fragments were listened to and when, at what point in the audio stream the participant switched to a different fragment, and how a fragment's rating was adjusted over time within a session, to name a few. Not only does this allow to evaluate a wealth of perceptual aspects, but it helps detect poor participants whose results are potentially not representative. 
241:     
242:     One of the key initial design parameters for WAET is to make the tool as open as possible to non-programmers and to this end the tool has been designed in such a way that all of the user modifiable options are included in a single XML document. This document is loaded up automatically by the web page and the JavaScript code parses and loads any extra resources required to create the test.
```

```
71: \begin{abstract}
72: A wearable AI assistant captures hours of egocentric video per day;
73: answering a look-back question (``where did I leave my keys?'')
74: requires retrieving the relevant moments under strict on-device
75: memory bounds. We propose \textbf{Probabilistic Spatial Memory}
76: (\psm), a streaming spatial-temporal index combining an H3 hex-grid
77: tessellation, a time-decayed ring buffer of HyperLogLog sketches per
78: cell, and reservoir-sampled CLIP-embedding exemplars. \psm{} exposes
79: a novel \caponek{} knob that smoothly trades strict spatial diversity
80: for embedding-similarity precision; the permissive endpoint
81: (\texttt{cap}=$K$) reduces to brute-force retrieval over all
82: in-reservoir exemplars. The
83: spatial-axis discrimination generalizes across \textbf{14 street-scale
84: sessions} drawn from \textbf{3 distinct sensor stacks} (SLOPER4D
85: head-mounted LiDAR, Nymeria + LookOut~\cite{pan2025lookout} Project
86: Aria MPS) and \textbf{3 encoder families} (laion CLIP-L / CLIP-bigG,
87: Google SigLIP~2~\cite{tschannen2025siglip2}): 13/14 sessions pass a
88: monotone-r10$\to$r12 Hit\,@\,5 acceptance with $\geq 4$\,pp lift on
89: at least one encoder. At matched candidate budget ($K{=}8$),
90: \psm{} \emph{beats} vanilla Gemini~3.1~Pro retrieval by
91: $1{-}\infty\times$ on every one of these 14 sessions (median
92: $\sim 4\times$, with 4 sessions where vanilla MLLM Hit\,@\,5 is
93: zero because the uniform $K{=}8$ frames structurally never land
94: in a $\sim$3\,s GT interval). The C engine ($\sim$700 LoC) and
95: Python eval harness are released under MIT.
```

```
173: deposited into the H3 hex cell containing its $(\text{lat},
174: \text{lng})$. Per-cell state is \emph{bounded}: a ring buffer of $C$
175: HyperLogLog sketches (orange; older sketches faded) gives a
176: time-decayed unique-event cardinality and the
177: $(t_{\min}, t_{\max})$ envelope; a reservoir of $R$
178: sampled embeddings (blue) is the bounded-memory substitute for the
179: linearly-growing CLIP bank.
180: Stage~2 (\emph{retrieval}): the query text is encoded with the same
181: encoder and cosine-similarity-searched against the reservoir union;
182: \caponek{} bounds how many of the $K{=}5$ slots a single cell may
183: fill, returning candidate $(t, \text{cell}, \text{lat}, \text{lng},
184: \mathbf{e})$ tuples in sub-millisecond C-side wall time.
185: Stage~3 (\emph{rerank}): the $K{=}5$ frames are fetched from the
186: device frame buffer and shipped to a frontier MLLM (Gemini\,3.1\,Pro),
187: which picks the single best frame index --- the localized answer.}
188: \label{fig:f1-architecture}
189: \end{figure}
```

```
15: Saturn's moon \titan{} is the only known world beyond Earth with stable
16: surface liquids, a dense organic-rich atmosphere, and a subsurface water
17: reservoir, making it a site where prebiotic chemistry can be studied at
18: planetary scale over geological time.  Previous habitability assessments
19: have been largely qualitative or restricted to a single location or epoch.
20: This thesis develops the first quantitative, spatially-resolved, multi-epoch
21: habitability map of \titan{}'s surface, combining eight Cassini observational
22: proxy features (liquid hydrocarbon, organic abundance, chemical energy,
23: methane cycling, surface--atmosphere exchange, topographic complexity,
24: geomorphological diversity, and subsurface water access) within a Bayesian
25: Beta-conjugate framework.  The posterior habitability probability
26: $P(H \mid \featurevec)$ is evaluated at every pixel of a global grid
27: (\SI{4490}{\metre\per\text{px}}, 6.49 million pixels) at five temporal anchor
28: epochs from the Late Heavy Bombardment ($-3.5\gya$) to the red-giant ocean
29: ($+5.9\gya$), with 95\% credible intervals at each location.

32: environments: Towada Lacus ranks first ($P(H) = 0.573$), driven by the highest
33: spectrally resolved organic abundance of any polar lake combined with surface
34: liquid and active methane cycling.  The temporal trajectory is non-monotonic,
35: passing through three regimes: organic-accumulation dominance during the
```

```
4: \chapter{Introduction}
5: \label{ch:introduction}
6: 
7: \section{Titan as an Astrobiological Target}
8: \label{sec:search_context}
9: 
10: The search for habitable environments beyond Earth has increasingly focused on icy ocean worlds in the outer solar system.  Among these, Saturn's moon \titan{} is unusual in several respects.
11: It is the only moon with a dense atmosphere (dominated by molecular nitrogen
12: at 1.467\,bar surface pressure and 93.65\,K; \citealt{Fulchignoni2005}, Appendix~\ref{app:constants}) and the
13: only known extraterrestrial world to host stable surface liquids
14: \citep{Stofan2007}, completing a full precipitation--evaporation--lake cycle
15: structurally analogous to Earth's hydrological cycle.  Its atmosphere
16: continuously produces complex organic tholins at
17: $\sim5\times10^{-14}$\,g\,cm$^{-2}$\,s$^{-1}$ \citep{Lavvas2011}, building
18: a global organic sediment layer over $\sim$4\,Gyr \citep{Lorenz2008}.
19: At depth, a subsurface water body at $\sim$55--80\,km was inferred from the
20: tidal Love number $k_2 = 0.589\pm0.150$ \citep{Iess2012}.  A 2025 reanalysis of the same Cassini radiometric data found interior tidal dissipation of $\sim$3--4\,TW inconsistent with a continuous global ocean, pointing instead to a thick slushy high-pressure ice layer with isolated pockets of liquid water \citep{Petricca2025}.  Tidal heating within this slushy layer maintains liquid water pockets and may generate brine conduits through the ice shell, as investigated by \citet{charlotte}. The subsurface water access precondition used in this thesis (Section~\ref{sec:defining_habitability}) is constructed to be agnostic to this distinction: it depends on tidally-driven conduits reaching the surface, a mechanism both the continuous-ocean and slushy-pocket models support (Section~\ref{sec:features}). Together, the cycling solvent, the large organic inventory, and the subsurface water make \titan{} a site where prebiotic chemistry can be studied at planetary scale over geological time.
21: 
22: \section{The Physical Environment}
23: \label{sec:titan_environment}
24: 
25: The atmosphere ($\sim$94\% \ce{N2}, 5.65\% \ce{CH4}; \citealt{Niemann2005})
26: sustains a methane cycle with observed equatorial rainfall \citep{Turtle2011},
27: fluvial channel networks \citep{Miller2021channels}, and polar hydrocarbon
28: seas (Kraken, Ligeia, and Punga Mare) containing $\sim$70{,}000\,km$^3$ of
29: liquid methane--ethane \citep{Mastrogiuseppe2019,Malaska2025}.  The lake distribution is markedly asymmetric: the north polar region hosts hundreds of filled lakes and seas covering $\sim$1.6\% of the global surface, while equivalent southern latitudes are largely devoid of standing liquid \citep{Aharonson2009}.  This hemispheric imbalance arises from the eccentricity of Saturn's orbit, which makes northern summers longer and milder than southern summers, driving net methane transport from south to north over Milankovitch-like cycles of $\sim$45{,}000\,yr \citep{Aharonson2009}.  The 45{,}000\,yr oscillation is far shorter than the spacing between the epochs modelled in this thesis (Section~\ref{sec:scope}), so the present-epoch north-polar dominance shown in the habitability maps should be read as a snapshot of the current phase of this cycle, not a permanent feature of \titan{}'s surface.  The surface is geologically diverse: equatorial dune fields ($\sim$17\% by SAR area), plains
30: ($\sim$65\%), labyrinth terrain, impact craters, and mountains, as classified
31: by the \citet{Lopes2019} global geomorphological map that
32: provides the terrain classification underpinning this thesis.
```

```
10: The framework proceeds in four analytical steps: (1) extraction of eight habitability-proxy features from the Cassini observational archive (Section~\ref{sec:features}); (2) Bayesian conjugate updating to produce a posterior habitability probability map at each epoch (Section~\ref{sec:bayes}); (3) temporal scaling of features across five anchor epochs and 74 intermediate geological epochs from $-3.8\gya$ to $+6.5\gya$ (Sections~\ref{sec:temporal_configs}--\ref{sec:multi_epoch}); and (4) ranking of named surface sites by posterior probability. 7: \label{ch:results}
```
```
8: 
9: \section{Overview and Temporal Habitability Trends}
10: \label{sec:results_overview}
11: 
12: The Bayesian framework produces posterior mean habitability maps $P(H \mid \featurevec)$ at five temporal anchor epochs and, via the multi-epoch reconstruction (Section~\ref{sec:multi_epoch}), at 74 intermediate epochs spanning $-3.8$ to $+6.5\gya$. The 95\% CI for Selk crater (the most-studied individual site) is $[0.04, 0.49]$, representative of the wide credible intervals arising from the moderate information content of the Cassini observables. 14: Figure~\ref{fig:temporal_trend} shows the temporal trajectory. The global mean then rises to its maximum of 0.530 at the \textit{Future} epoch ($+5.9\gya$) as the red-giant ocean covers the surface.
```

```
117: % estimated $\sim$70{,}000\,km$^3$ of liquid methane--ethane--nitrogen, and a
118: % deep interior water--ammonia ocean inferred from tidal deformation
119: % measurements.  This convergence of chemical feedstock, cycling solvent, and
120: % liquid environments makes \titan{} not merely a potentially habitable world
121: % but a natural laboratory for prebiotic chemistry at planetary scale.
122: 
123: % This thesis presents a quantitative, spatially-resolved probabilistic
124: % framework for assessing \titan{}'s surface and near-surface habitability at
125: % five temporal configurations spanning the Late Heavy Bombardment
126: % ($-3.5\gya$), a lake-formation transition epoch ($-1.0\gya$), the
```

```
8: \section{Background and Motivation}
9: \label{sec:motivation}
10: 
11: For most of computing history, the only ``language'' a machine could be made to
12: understand with any depth was source code, and even that understanding was
13: trapped inside individual tools. An editor that knew how to complete a Python
14: symbol knew nothing about Rust; a tool that could navigate Java could not hover
15: over TypeScript. Each pair of an editor and a programming language demanded its
16: own integration, so that supporting $M$ editors across $N$ languages implied, in
17: the worst case, $M \times N$ separate implementations of the same handful of
18: ideas: completion, go-to-definition, diagnostics, hover.
19: 
20: In 2016, Microsoft, Red Hat, and Codenvy published the \emph{Language Server
21: Protocol} (LSP), a JSON-RPC contract that let a single \emph{language server}
22: serve any number of editors \citep{lsp-redhat-2016,lsp-official}. The protocol's
23: own documentation states the design intent plainly: ``a single Language Server
24: can be re-used in multiple development tools, which in turn can support multiple
25: languages with minimal effort'' \citep{lsp-official}. The combinatorial effect
26: is the move from $M \times N$ to $M + N$: $M$ editor adapters plus $N$ servers
27: \citep{lsp-mxn-fcc}. LSP did not make editors smarter; it \emph{decoupled} the
28: locus of language intelligence from the locus of display, and in doing so turned
29: ``understanding a language'' into a reusable, networked service.
```

```
1: \chapter{Mathematical Foundations, from First Principles}
2: \label{ch:math}
3: 
4: \epigraph{Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different
5: things.}{Henri Poincar\'e}
6: 
7: The arguments of this thesis---that three protocols compose into one substrate,
8: that conformance is three-valued, that convergence is a phase transition, that a
9: repository can be read as a curved space of trajectories---are stated informally
10: in \cref{ch:framework} and instantiated in \cref{ch:artifact}. This chapter
11: supplies their mathematics, and it does so \emph{from first principles}: each
12: construct is built from sets and axioms, with definitions, and with proofs of the
13: propositions the later chapters invoke. The intent is that no subsequent claim
14: rests on borrowed authority; where the thesis says ``composition'', ``lattice'',
15: ``latent heat'', or ``curvature'', this chapter says exactly what is meant.
16: 
17: We make no claim to new mathematics. The contribution is the \emph{derivation of
18: the thesis's own constructs} within standard mathematics, so that they are
19: falsifiable rather than merely evocative. Five pillars are built, and a short
20: synthesis (\cref{sec:synthesis-functor}) draws them into a single functor; each
21: terminates in a result used later:
22: 
23: \begin{description}[leftmargin=1.6em,style=nextline]
24:   \item[Pillar I --- The algebra of composition (\cref{sec:alg}).] From monoids
25:   through categories, functors, adjunctions, monoidal categories, and operads to
26:   the \emph{Decoupling Theorem} (\cref{thm:decoupling}), which is the algebraic
27:   engine behind the phase transition's mechanism (\cref{prop:discontinuous}).
28:   \item[Pillar II --- The order-theoretic logic of conformance.] From posets and
29:   lattices to Kleene's and Belnap's many-valued logics, formalising the
30:   \code{ConformanceVector} (\cref{lst:cv}) and \cref{prin:three-valued}.
31:   \item[Pillar III --- The analysis of phase transitions.] From limits and
32:   continuity to Landau's free-energy expansion and a from-scratch derivation of
33:   the Clausius--Clapeyron relation and the latent heat that anchors
34:   \cref{sec:fw-latent}.
35:   \item[Pillar IV --- The geometry of law-state.] From topological spaces through
36:   smooth manifolds, connections, and curvature to gradient flow, formalising the
37:   manifold metaphors of \code{AGENTS.md} (repository as manifold, failsets as
38:   curvature, admissibility as $\Phi_G = 0$).
39:   \item[Pillar V --- Measure, probability, and information.] From $\sigma$-algebras
40:   through entropy and Fisher information, making ``receipts are proof measure'' a
41:   literal measure, recasting non-collapse as a data-processing inequality, and
42:   identifying the manifold of Pillar~IV with a statistical manifold via the
43:   Fisher--Rao metric.
44: \end{description}
45: 
46: A reader fluent in these areas may treat the chapter as fixing notation and skip
47: to \cref{ch:framework}; a reader who wants the thesis to stand on its own will
48: find here the load it is asked to bear. Pillars are developed in the order above;
49: forward references to later chapters are deliberate, marking where each piece of
```

```
187: \markboth{Abstract}{Abstract}

189: The Language Server Protocol (LSP) decoupled editors from language intelligence,
190: collapsing an $M \times N$ integration burden into $M + N$ and turning code
191: understanding into a reusable service \citep{lsp-redhat-2016,lsp-official}.
192: A decade later, two further protocols have repeated this move at higher layers:
193: the Model Context Protocol (MCP), open-sourced by Anthropic in November~2024,
194: standardised how models reach tools, data, and context \citep{mcp-anthropic-2024};
195: and the Agent-to-Agent protocol (A2A), published by Google in April~2025,
196: standardised how autonomous agents discover and coordinate with one another
197: \citep{a2a-google-2025}. This thesis argues that the fusion of these three
198: protocols---LSP for meaning, MCP for context, A2A for coordination---constitutes
199: not an incremental integration but a \emph{phase transition} in machine-mediated
200: language, analogous to the roughly $1{,}600$--$1{,}700$-fold volume expansion when
201: water becomes steam at its boiling point \citep{phys-illinois-steam,nationalboard-steam}.
202: The input that drives the transition is standardisation: a large, discontinuous
203: investment---a latent heat---absorbed at apparent constant ``temperature'' that,
204: once paid, expands the addressable surface of language by orders of magnitude.
205: 
206: We develop the argument through the lens of process mining, the discipline
207: founded by Wil van der Aalst, in which behaviour recorded as event logs is checked
208: for conformance against a model of how it ought to unfold
209: \citep{pm-manifesto-2011,vdaalst-book-2016}. We contend that when LSP is
210: generalised beyond source code to all forms of language---natural language,
211: legal and regulatory text, mathematics, biological sequence, music, and business
212: process---each such language acquires an event log and therefore a conformance
213: surface. Echoing van der Aalst's recent dictum that there is ``no AI without PI''
214: (process intelligence), in which object-centric process mining is ``the missing
215: link connecting data and processes'' \citep{noai-nopi-2025}, we argue that there
216: is no trustworthy conformance for all language without an object-centric event
217: abstraction \citep{ocel2-2024}.
218: 
219: We instantiate the argument in \lspmax, a law-state runtime projected through LSP
220: whose \code{ConformanceVector} keeps \admitted, \refused, and \unknownstat{} law
221: axes strictly distinct, whose diagnostics are emitted as object-centric events
222: (OCEL~2.0), and whose claims are graded only by bounded status \citep{lspmax}.
223: Using design-science methodology \citep{hevner2004,peffers2007}, we present the
224: artifact, a fusion architecture, and a 2030 roadmap. Throughout, we adopt the
225: artifact's own epistemic discipline: we grade each claim as \admitted, \refused,
226: or \unknownstat; we mark every projection as a \forecast; and we decline the
227: language of triumph.
228:

230: \noindent\textbf{Keywords:} process mining; conformance checking; object-centric
231: event logs; Language Server Protocol; Model Context Protocol; Agent-to-Agent
232: protocol; agentic AI; law-state runtime; protocol convergence.

239: This thesis studies an artifact, \lspmax, whose constitution forbids
240: \emph{victory language}---unbounded declarations such as ``solved'' or
241: ``guaranteed''---and instead requires every claim to carry a \emph{bounded
242: status} and, where admission is asserted, a \emph{receipt}: a content-addressed
243: record binding a digest, a boundary, and a negative-control result
244: \citep{lspmax}. It would be inconsistent to describe such an artifact in the
245: register it refuses. We therefore adopt its discipline as our own. Findings are
246: graded \admitted{} (evidence present and checked), \refused{} (evidence present,
247: contrary), or \unknownstat{} (admissibility not yet determinable); intermediate
248: grades \candidate, \partialstat, and \openstat{} are used where appropriate. The
249: three states never collapse into one another: an \unknownstat{} is never quietly
250: promoted to \admitted. Numerical predictions about 2030 are commercial or
251: analyst forecasts, not measurements, and are marked \forecast. Quotations from
252: primary specifications are reproduced verbatim and cited to the revision in force
253: at the time of writing; the reader is cautioned that living specifications
254: (MCP, A2A, and LSP~3.18 among them) continue to evolve.
```

```
236: \addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{A Note on Method and Language}
237: \markboth{A Note on Method and Language}{A Note on Method and Language}
238: 
239: This thesis studies an artifact, \lspmax, whose constitution forbids
240: \emph{victory language}---unbounded declarations such as ``solved'' or
241: ``guaranteed''---and instead requires every claim to carry a \emph{bounded
242: status} and, where admission is asserted, a \emph{receipt}: a content-addressed
243: record binding a digest, a boundary, and a negative-control result
244: \citep{lspmax}. It would be inconsistent to describe such an artifact in the
245: register it refuses. We therefore adopt its discipline as our own. Findings are
246: graded \admitted{} (evidence present and checked), \refused{} (evidence present,
247: contrary), or \unknownstat{} (admissibility not yet determinable); intermediate
248: grades \candidate, \partialstat, and \openstat{} are used where appropriate. The
249: three states never collapse into one another: an \unknownstat{} is never quietly
250: promoted to \admitted. Numerical predictions about 2030 are commercial or
251: analyst forecasts, not measurements, and are marked \forecast. Quotations from
252: primary specifications are reproduced verbatim and cited to the revision in force
253: at the time of writing; the reader is cautioned that living specifications
254: (MCP, A2A, and LSP~3.18 among them) continue to evolve.
```

```
1: Algorithmic fairness has become critical as machine learning systems deploy in high-stakes domains. A common approach enforces fairness constraints during training, such as Demographic Parity (DP)---equal positive prediction rates across protected groups---and Individual Fairness (IF)---similar individuals receiving similar predictions \citep{hardt2016equality,dwork2012fairness}.
2: 
3: Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) offers a principled framework for robustness to distributional shifts. DRO-FAIR formulates fairness as a constraint within DRO, learning parameters that satisfy fairness under the worst-case distribution within an uncertainty set \citep{hashimoto2018fairness}.
4: 
5: \textbf{The Gap.} Existing evaluations use \textit{random label noise}---uniformly flipping labels. This does not reflect adversarial scenarios where an attacker with knowledge of the fairness metric strategically corrupts the most impactful samples \citep{solans2021poisoning}. To our knowledge, no prior work computes the \textbf{exact gradient} of fairness metrics with respect to individual labels.
6: 
7: \textbf{Our Contributions.}
8: (1) \textit{FairnessTargetedPGD}: gradient-based attacks computing
9: $\partial(\text{fairness})/\partial y_i$ on each label.
10: (2) The temperature ablation: fixing $\tau=1$ across all $\alpha$ (vs.\
11: the stepped $\tau{=}100$ schedule for $\alpha\le 0.3$) is the
12: single biggest determinant of whether DRO wins or loses on Adult DP
13: under adversarial attack.
14: (3) The IF k-NN ablation and the empirical-radii interpretation per
15: Kuldeep's feedback (\S\ref{sec:results-tabular}).
16: (4) The adversarial-vs-random comparison showing adversarial PGD
17: raises DP by an order of magnitude more than random label noise at
18: matched $\alpha$ on Adult.
```

```
1: \subsection{Threat Model}
2: The attacker modifies fraction $\alpha$ of training labels, features, and protected attributes, with white-box access to the fairness metric.
3: 
4: \subsection{DP-only Attack}
5: The gradient of the DP gap with respect to each label is:
6: \begin{equation}
7: \frac{\partial (\text{DP}_{\text{gap}})}{\partial y_i} = \text{sign}(\bar{y}_0 - \bar{y}_1) \times \left(\frac{\mathbf{1}\{a_i=0\}}{n_0} - \frac{\mathbf{1}\{a_i=1\}}{n_1}\right)
8: \end{equation}
9: where $\bar{y}_g$ is the mean label for group $g$. We flip the top-$\alpha n$ samples with the largest positive gradient.
10: 
11: \subsection{IF-only Attack}
12: Using a $k$-NN graph within each protected group:
13: \begin{equation}
14: \frac{\partial (\text{IF})}{\partial y_i} = \frac{\text{agree}_i - \text{disagree}_i}{k_{\text{eff}}}
15: \end{equation}
16: 
17: \subsection{PGD Optimization}
18: We run $\mathrm{pgd\_steps}{=}20$ iterative steps: (1) compute the
19: fairness-metric gradient with respect to each label and feature
20: perturbation (the feature-perturbation half maximises $|p_0-p_1|$
21: directly for the DP and combined attacks, and falls back to
22: classification loss only for the IF attack), (2) rank samples by
23: gradient magnitude, (3) flip the top-$\alpha$ labels, (4) repeat.
24: After all steps we enforce the exact $\alpha$ budget by keeping
25: only the top-$\alpha$ flips ranked by final gradient magnitude.
26: The IF attack uses a k-NN graph ($k{=}5$ default; the ablation in
27: \S\ref{sec:results-tabular} shows the attack is insensitive to $k$).
```

```
1: \subsection{The Temperature ($\tau$) Effect}
2: \label{sec:tau-discussion}
3: 
4: Our central finding on the tabular side is that the prediction
5: soft-max temperature $\tau$ is the dominant knob for whether DRO
6: wins or loses on Adult DP.  Under a stepped schedule
7: ($\tau{=}100$ for $\alpha\le 0.3$, $\tau{=}1$ for $\alpha{=}0.4$)
8: DRO loses on Adult DP almost everywhere; under a fixed $\tau{=}1$
9: schedule DRO wins on Adult DP at every $\alpha$ and the gap widens
10: monotonically.  This is consistent with the theory: $\tau{=}100$
11: sharpens the predictions toward $0$/$1$ and so makes the inner
12: re-weighting concentrate weights on a few ``worst'' samples,
13: driving $\lambda_{\mathrm{DP}}$ to its clamp and causing the
14: $\lambda$-runaway the earlier ``adversarial feedback loop''
15: discussion was observing.  At $\tau{=}1$ the soft predictions
16: distribute weight smoothly and $\lambda$ stays bounded, so the
17: re-weighting helps rather than hurts.
18: 
19: \subsection{Adversarial vs.\ Random Corruption}
20: The empirical comparison (\texttt{results/random\_vs\_adversarial\_new.json})
21: confirms that adversarial PGD raises DP $12$--$40\times$ more than
22: random label noise at matched $\alpha$ on Adult, and $2$--$22\times$
23: on Credit.  This rules out the ``attack is too weak''
24: counter-explanation for the Adult low-$\alpha$ cells.
25: 
26: \subsection{Mechanism (old ``feedback loop'')}
27: The earlier ``adversarial feedback loop'' account of Adult
28: $\alpha\ge 0.3$ (DRO collapsing to constant predictions) is no
29: longer the right diagnosis under $\tau{=}1$.  We do still see lower
30: accuracy at $\alpha{=}0.4$ ($\approx 0.55$ for both Naive and DRO
31: on Adult under DP attack), but DP and accuracy are now both
32: controlled rather than trading against each other.
33: 
34: \subsection{Empirical Radii (Q5)}
35: The TV-radius formula
36: $\rho_{\mathrm{DP},j}=\alpha/((1-\alpha)\pi_j+\alpha)$ and the
37: bias-corrected $\hat\pi_{j,\mathrm{clean}}=(\hat\pi_j-\alpha)/(1-2\alpha)$
38: are empirical, not theoretical.  Under our coordinated (70\%-minority)
39: attack structure they can be tightened by estimating $\pi_{\mathrm{clean}}$
40: from the observed post-attack group proportions directly.  We
41: implement this as \texttt{radii\_mode='empirical'} in
42: \texttt{src/training/dro\_fair.py} (default stays 'uniform').  This
43: is in line with Kuldeep's Q5 ("if the attack is known then we can
44: use this approximation according to the attack") and does not claim
45: the paper is wrong.
46: 
47: \subsection{Image data (UTKFace) --- pending GPU access}
48: The earlier "DRO inverts on ResNet18 features" claim from prior
49: versions of this paper was based on tau=100-stepped results and is
50: withdrawn.  We have no tau=1 UTKFace results yet because the
51: flair2 GPU access is unresolved.  See \S\ref{sec:results-utkface}.
52:
```

```
1: \chapter{Related Work}
2: \label{ch:related-work}
3: 
4: \section{Image Classification with Neural Network}
5: \label{sec:image-classification-with-neural-network}
6: 
7: One of the first instances where Neural Network were employed for image
8: classification was in 1998 by Lecun et al.~\cite{GradientBasedLecun1998}. Their
9: model, LeNet-5, was able to identify handwritten digit with higher accuracy
10: than previous methods which relied on manual features extraction such edges
11: detection and hard-coded pattern recognition. A raw image of a digit is passed
12: as input to LeNet and the model spits out a number from 0 to 9. Some
13: foundational ideas were at the core of the architecture (convolutional
14: operations, gradient based optimization, pooling layers) stood the test of time
15: and proved to be highly successful.
16: 
17: Fast forwarding to 2012. AlexNet~\cite{ImagenetClassiKrizhe2017}, a
18: \acrfull{cnn} similar in spirit to LeNet-5, annihilated competitions at
19: \acrfull{ilsvrc}~\cite{ImagenetLargeRussak2014} with a whopping 10.8 \% gap on
20: the runner-up in top-5 error metric. This result proved the potential of
21: \acrshort{cnn}s to process bigger color images (224 × 224 × 3) and this sparked
22: interest in the field which abandoned the idea of manual features extraction in
23: favour of the end-to-end approach.
24: 
25: Researchers investigated various moving part of \acrshort{cnn} architecture:
26: depth of the model, optimal kernel size, number of filters, pooling operations.
27: \cite{VeryDeepConvoSimony2014,GoingDeeperWiSzeged2014} focus on increasing the
28: depth of the models and \cite{GoingDeeperWiSzeged2014} was able to do so by the
29: introduction of a highly efficient ``Inception module'' which was able to
30: increase the depth while keeping the FLOPs under control. Efficiency at
31: inference time is crucial for embedding models into resource constrained
32: devices such smartphones or IOTs~\cite{SqueezenetAleIandol2016,
33: MnasnetPlatfoTanM2018, MobilenetsEffHoward2017}.
34: 
35: A problem that arose with the increase in depth was the so-called ``vanishing
36: gradient''. The gradient of the loss function with respect to the model's
37: parameters in the early layers tends to zero and this affect the ability of the
38: optimizer to update the weights towards a local minimum. Residual connections,
39: introduced in ResNet~\cite{DeepResidualLHeKa2015, IdentityMappinHeKa2016}, are
40: shortcuts in the network architecture that circumvent the problem allowing the
41: gradient to flow backwards effectively, so deeper models can be trained.
42: Connections between layers, i.e. the topology of the network, was further
43: explored by~\cite{DualPathNetwoChen2017, DenselyConnectHuang2016} and prior
44: using evolutionary methods by~\cite{DesigningNeuraMiller1989,
45: EvolvingNeuralStanle2002}.
46: 
47: Neural Architecture Search was employed to search for the width and the depth
48: of a model given a basic building block~\cite{ProgressiveNeuLiuC2017,
49: GeneticCnnXieL2017, LargeScaleEvoReal2017, RegularizedEvoReal2018}. Using
50: different building blocks and optimizing for different budget types (e.g.
51: FLOPs, number of parameters, inference time) various architecture were
52: produced. EfficientNets~\cite{EfficientnetRTanM2019, Efficientnetv2TanM2021}
53: are a well-known example of such approach that make use of
54: Squeeze-and-Excitation module~\cite{SqueezeAndExcHuJi2017} as basic component.
55: 
56: Stacks of convolution blocks followed by a fully connected layers start to
57: reach the limit regarding classification accuracy. \acrshort{cnn}s were
58: equipped with an attention mechanism be able to effectively process global
59: features in an image defining hybrid
60: architecture~\cite{SpatialTransfoJaderb2015, LookAndThinkCaoC2015,
61: ShowAttendAnXuKe2015, ScaCnnSpatiaChen2016}. Recently interest shifted towards
62: Vision Transformers (ViT)~\cite{AnImageIsWorDosovi2020}, architecture that use
63: solely attention mechanism for features extraction which are able to achieve
64: state-of-the-art results in some well-established image classification
65: problems~\cite{TransformersInKhan2021, ASurveyOnVisHanK2023}. ViT required to
66: be trained of huge datasets to achieve competitive performance and, at the
67: moment of the writing, cannot run on consumer and low power devices due to high
68: computational cost.
69: 
70: \section{Semantic Information Representations}
71: \label{sec:semantic-information-sources}
72: Image classification consists in assigning a label to an image given a fixed
73: set of labels. Without any additional information about labels they are just a
74: set of symbols with no structure nor relationship between them. On the other
75: hand having richer information on labels turns out to be beneficial for model
76: interpretability~\cite{ImprovingInterDong2017}, image
77: summarization~\cite{SemanticImagePasini2022} and image classification as
78: well~\cite{MakingBetterMBertin2019}. Assuming that label a label of an image is
79: an English word indicating what is depicted in the image, we can obtain extra
80: information about a label by various sources which produce different
81: representations.
82: 
83: \paragraph{Hierarchies (trees)}
84: \label{par:hierarchies-tree}
85: WordNet~\cite{WordnetMi1995} is a lexical database for the English language
86: where words are linked together by semantic relations (synonyms, hyponyms and
87: meronyms) resulting in a graph structure. The aforementioned ImageNet database
88: was build using WordNet as a source of labels, so information from WordNet could
89: be exploited when training a model on ImageNet. Other examples of semantically
90: enriched datasets include iNaturalist~\cite{TheInaturalistHorn2017} (taxonomy)
91: and CIFAR-100~\cite{LearningMultipKrizhe2009} (handcrafted). Given a graph
92: structure, it can be pruned in such a way to obtain a rooted tree, that is a
93: connected acyclic undirected graph with one vertex as root. Moreover, we can
94: assign a natural orientation to edges towards (or away from) the root. The
95: resulting data structure can be used to represent hierarchical organised
96: knowledge such ontologies or taxonomies.
97: 
98: \paragraph{Embeddings (vectors)}
99: \label{par:embeddings-vectors}
100: The majority of times labels are just a set of words with no structure between,
101: so semantic structure has to be constructed from bare words. A flexible
102: approach is to resort to internal representation of a pre-trained \acrfull{lm}
103: commonly knows as word embeddings~\cite{BeyondWordEmbIncitt2023}. The extracted
104: semantic structure is organised as a vector space where words are represented
105: as real-valued vectors. The input to a \acrshort{lm} can be the raw label or a
106: detailed description of the label. Additionally, such a description can be
107: written by human experts, scrape from the web or generated by a \acrshort{lm}
108: itself.\medskip
109: 
110: These two approaches produce different representations of semantic information
111: (tree vs vectors) so exist different ways to inject it into a model. It is
```

```
14: operations, gradient based optimization, pooling layers) stood the test of time
15: and proved to be highly successful.
16:

18: \acrfull{cnn} similar in spirit to LeNet-5, annihilated competitions at
19: \acrfull{ilsvrc}~\cite{ImagenetLargeRussak2014} with a whopping 10.8 \% gap on
20: the runner-up in top-5 error metric. This result proved the potential of
21: \acrshort{cnn}s to process bigger color images (224 × 224 × 3) and this sparked
22: interest in the field which abandoned the idea of manual features extraction in
23: favour of the end-to-end approach.
24: 
25: Researchers investigated various moving part of \acrshort{cnn} architecture:
26: depth of the model, optimal kernel size, number of filters, pooling operations.
27: \cite{VeryDeepConvoSimony2014,GoingDeeperWiSzeged2014} focus on increasing the
28: depth of the models and \cite{GoingDeeperWiSzeged2014} was able to do so by the
29: introduction of a highly efficient ``Inception module'' which was able to
30: increase the depth while keeping the FLOPs under control. Efficiency at
31: inference time is crucial for embedding models into resource constrained
32: devices such smartphones or IOTs~\cite{SqueezenetAleIandol2016,
33: MnasnetPlatfoTanM2018, MobilenetsEffHoward2017}.

36: gradient''. The gradient of the loss function with respect to the model's
37: parameters in the early layers tends to zero and this affect the ability of the
38: optimizer to update the weights towards a local minimum. Residual connections,
39: introduced in ResNet~\cite{DeepResidualLHeKa2015, IdentityMappinHeKa2016}, are
40: shortcuts in the network architecture that circumvent the problem allowing the
41: gradient to flow backwards effectively, so deeper models can be trained.

43: explored by~\cite{DualPathNetwoChen2017, DenselyConnectHuang2016} and prior
44: using evolutionary methods by~\cite{DesigningNeuraMiller1989,
```

\subsection{Metavariable Substitution}
Metavariable substitution takes a term $t$ in $\Delta$ with holes in $H$, and a function $f$ (called a meta substitution) sending holes in $H$ over $\Gamma$ to terms in $\Gamma, \Delta$ with holes in $S$.
It produces a term in $\Delta$ with holes in $S$.

Much like CAS, it acts recursively on each term constructor.
On variables, it is the identity function, directly returning the variable.
On application, it recurses down both sides of the application.
On abstraction (and any binder), it weakens $f$ to produce a meta substitution $f'$, sending holes in $H$ over $\Gamma, x$ to terms in $\Gamma, \Delta, x$ with holes in $S$.
We then perform metavariable substitution on the body of the abstraction with $f'$.

The metavariable case is, naturally, the most complex.
Given a metavariable $?m[\theta]$, where $\theta : \Delta \to \Gamma$, the algorithm is as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item Perform metavariable substitution with $f$ on $\theta$ to get a substitution $\theta'$ with holes in $S$ instead of $H$.
\item Take the identity substitution in $\Delta$, and extend it with $\theta'$ to get a substitution $\theta''$ that maps $\Gamma, \Delta$ to $\Delta$, with holes in $S$.
\item Look up $m$ in $f$ to produce $t$, a term in $\Gamma, \Delta$ with holes in $S$.
\item Perform capture-avoiding substitution on $t$ with the substitution $\theta''$.

Meta substitution is a form of monadic bind.

\item Look up $m$ in $f$ to produce $t$, a term in $\Gamma ++ \Delta$ with holes in $S$.
\item Perform capture-avoiding substitution on $t$ with the renaming $\theta''$.
